BIE task prefix understand.read_page/4 · rulebook canvas_profile@2026-10-27.2+content_types@2026-10-27.1+explanations@2026-10-24.1+level_profiles@2026-10-24.1+simple_hindi@2026-10-27.1+teacher_examples@2026-10-27.1+vision-2026-10-21@2026-10-21.14+visual_grammar@2026-10-26.2+visual_levels@2026-10-26.2 · content types 2026-10-27.1 · schema bie.brain.understand-page/4

You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Indian Economy for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "3. Money" · subject: Indian Economy · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.
[S1-16] Apply every economics concept in the real world first (Navin, 27 October 2026): in a chapter of the economics family, every definition, cause_effect and process item carries in its unpack a real_world_example: a place (bazaar, kirana shop, mandi, bank, factory, petrol pump, farm), actors (shopkeeper, buyers, farmer, worker, bank, RBI, government), real goods or money (sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI), numbers that change (before → after) and at least two steps, each mapped to a link of the concept's mechanism; then the sentence that names the term after the story, and one line on where the learner meets it in real life. The example is economically correct (the mechanism it runs is the concept's) and fits the learner's level (UPSC: the real Indian link, for example repo rate → home-loan EMI, only from the book or a dated source). Navin's example: a kirana shop with 3 packets of sugar at ₹50, buyers 2 → 12, the price ₹65, only 3 can buy: demand-pull inflation.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
  - unpack.real_world_example (S1-16; Navin, 27 October 2026: "economic concepts ko real world mein apply karke samjhao"): in a chapter
    of the economics family, for every definition, cause_effect and process item, the concept APPLIED in an everyday Indian situation
    before it is named: place (bazaar, kirana shop, mandi, bank, factory, petrol pump, farm); actors (shopkeeper, buyers, farmer,
    worker, bank, RBI, government); goods (the real goods or money: sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI); numbers (each
    {what, before, after}, written with digits: {"what": "price", "before": "₹50", "after": "₹65"}, {"what": "buyers", "before": "2",
    "after": "12"}); steps (at least two, each {step, mechanism_link}: the story step by step, and the link of the concept's mechanism
    that step shows); term_after (the sentence that names the term only after the story: "isliye ise demand-pull inflation kehte
    hain"); real_life_link (one line on where the learner meets it; UPSC: the real Indian link, for example repo rate → home-loan EMI,
    only from the page or a dated source). The example must be economically correct: the mechanism it runs is the concept's, and the
    numbers move the way the concept says. Navin's example: a kirana shop with 3 packets of sugar at ₹50; buyers 2 → 12; the price
    ₹65; only 3 can buy: demand-pull inflation. BIE's code checks the place, an actor, the goods, a number that changes, two steps with
    their links, term_after and real_life_link. Every other item (another subject family, another type, a question, a heading) leaves
    it empty ("" and []).
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-27.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.
- Apply it in the real world first, then name it (Navin's sugar shop) (every economics concept (a definition, a cause-and-effect chain, a process): the example runs before the term is named): Ek kirana shop mein chini ke 3 packet hain, ₹50 ka ek. Kal 2 khareedar aaye the, aaj 12 aa gaye; sab ko chini chahiye par packet 3 hi hain. Dukandar daam ₹65 kar deta hai; ab sirf 3 log kharid paate hain, baaki 9 khaali haath. Zyada log, utna hi maal, isliye daam upar. Isliye ise demand-pull inflation kehte hain. Phir book ki definition. Phir: yahi aap Diwali se pehle sabzi mandi mein dekhte hain.

output.page_summary: Money is anything accepted for exchange and settling debts, including cash, bank deposits and digital balances. Good money has acceptability, durability, portability, divisibility, uniformity and limited supply. Its four core functions are medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.

items.content: Definition: Money is anything that is accepted as a medium of exchange for goods and services and for settling debts.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the defining test of money on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is accepted in exchange for goods and services and in settlement of debts; its role in payment, rather than a particular physical form, defines it.

teacher_understanding.question: Which wording shows that money need not be a particular object?
teacher_understanding.answer: The definition says 'anything that is accepted', and the following lines include bank deposits and digital balances as well as cash.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does acceptance matter more than an object's usefulness to its holder?
teacher_understanding.answer: A payment works only if the recipient will take it. A useful possession does not automatically allow its owner to buy other goods or discharge an obligation.

teacher_understanding.question: How do buying a service and settling a debt differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Buying a service pays for work supplied, such as a haircut; settling a debt clears an amount already owed, such as an earlier loan.

prerequisites: An amount owed to another person
items.exam_note: Test acceptance and payment function, not physical form or intrinsic usefulness.

terms.plain_meaning: जिसे देकर सामान या सेवा ले सकें
terms.everyday_image: दुकानदार को पैसे देकर चावल लेना

terms.plain_meaning: पहले का उधार चुका देना
terms.everyday_image: किराना दुकान की उधार वाली रकम चुकाना

why_chain.step: A buyer needs goods but the seller may not want the buyer's goods in return.
An accepted payment medium lets the buyer obtain goods and clear amounts owed.

unpack.example_or_place: A kirana purchase and repayment of shop credit.
unpack.consequence: Look for acceptance in payments before asking whether the money is cash or a balance.
unpack.visual_verb: Exchange goods for payment, then cross out an outstanding debt.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish an asset that is valuable from something accepted as money.

steps.step: The shopkeeper accepts ₹100 for rice.
steps.mechanism_link: Acceptance allows exchange for goods.

steps.step: The buyer pays another ₹50 to clear an earlier shop debt.
steps.mechanism_link: The same accepted medium settles an obligation.

real_world_example.term_after: The accepted means used for these purchases and repayments is money.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page's definition applies to shopping and clearing everyday dues.

items.content: Money is not just currency notes and coins.

teacher_understanding.question: What misconception does this statement reject?
teacher_understanding.answer: It rejects equating the whole of money with its physical currency forms.

teacher_understanding.question: What on the page establishes that money has non-cash forms?
teacher_understanding.answer: The next bullet explicitly includes bank deposits and digital balances.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can money exist without a note or coin changing hands?
teacher_understanding.answer: An accepted transfer of a monetary balance can complete payment without physical cash being passed across a counter.

items.exam_note: The claim 'money consists only of notes and coins' is the key trap.

terms.plain_meaning: हाथ में पकड़कर दिए जाने वाले नोट और सिक्के
terms.everyday_image: बटुए में रखा नोट और जेब के सिक्के

why_chain.step: A learner sees cash daily and may mistake its visible form for all money.
The book includes non-cash balances, so the category is wider than currency.

unpack.example_or_place: Paying from a bank balance instead of taking cash from a wallet.
unpack.consequence: Money should be recognised by its payment role, not merely its appearance.
unpack.visual_verb: Expand a cash-only circle to include balances.
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer that every financial asset is money merely because money includes more than currency.

items.content: It includes anything people widely accept for payments—cash, bank deposits, and digital balances.

teacher_understanding.question: Which payment forms does this page include?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cash, bank deposits and digital balances are the page's examples of widely accepted forms.

teacher_understanding.question: What criterion links the three examples?
teacher_understanding.answer: The line introduces them as things people widely accept for payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How should students distinguish a balance from the device used to spend it?
teacher_understanding.answer: The balance is the monetary amount available; a phone or payment application is a way to instruct a transfer. The device is not itself the money.

items.exam_note: Identify the listed forms without treating a payment application as an additional stock of money.

terms.plain_meaning: bank खाते में जमा रकम
terms.everyday_image: पासबुक में दिखती जमा रकम

terms.plain_meaning: डिजिटल तरीके से दर्ज और भुगतान में इस्तेमाल होने वाली रकम
terms.everyday_image: स्क्रीन पर दिखता उपलब्ध balance

why_chain.step: People need to pay even when they do not hand over physical currency.
Widely accepted deposits and digital balances are therefore included on the page.

unpack.example_or_place: A shop counter where payment can come from cash or an account balance.
unpack.consequence: Different forms can perform the same payment role.
unpack.visual_verb: Route three payment forms toward one shop purchase.
unpack.level_extra: The page is introductory: it does not classify monetary aggregates or different kinds of digital balances.

items.exam_note: The following six items carry the content.

items.content: Acceptability: Everyone is willing to accept it.

teacher_understanding.question: What does acceptability mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: People are willing to take the money offered to them in payment.

teacher_understanding.question: Which printed wording identifies willingness rather than physical quality?
teacher_understanding.answer: The characteristic is explained as 'Everyone is willing to accept it.'

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the recipient's willingness matter?
teacher_understanding.answer: If sellers refuse a proposed means of payment, possessing it does not help the buyer complete those purchases. Confidence that others will accept it supports its use.

items.exam_note: Acceptability concerns willingness to receive money, unlike portability or durability.

terms.plain_meaning: लोग उसे भुगतान में लेने को तैयार हों
terms.everyday_image: दुकानदार पैसे लेकर सामान दे देता है

why_chain.step: A buyer needs the seller to take the offered payment.
Willingness to accept it makes the proposed money usable in exchange.

unpack.example_or_place: A shopkeeper accepting payment for groceries.
unpack.consequence: Without acceptance, the exchange function cannot work effectively.
unpack.visual_verb: Accept payment and release the goods.
unpack.level_extra: Read 'Everyone' as the book's ideal characteristic; this is not a claim that every payment form is accepted at every counter.

steps.step: A buyer owes ₹100 for groceries and offers cash.
steps.mechanism_link: A payment medium must be offered to the recipient.

steps.step: The shopkeeper willingly takes it and marks the bill paid.
steps.mechanism_link: Recipient willingness enables completion of payment.

real_world_example.term_after: This willingness to receive the payment is acceptability.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page's characteristic is visible whenever a seller agrees to take a payment.

items.content: Durability: Does not wear out quickly.

teacher_understanding.question: What quality does durability describe?
teacher_understanding.answer: Money should remain usable rather than deteriorate quickly through handling or time.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the book state durability?
teacher_understanding.answer: It says good money 'Does not wear out quickly.'

teacher_understanding.question: Why does repeated use require durability?
teacher_understanding.answer: Money passes between people. A fragile or perishable payment object would need frequent replacement and might cease to be acceptable after deterioration.

prerequisites: Money passing from one holder to another
items.exam_note: Durability concerns physical persistence, not protection against inflation.

terms.plain_meaning: बार-बार इस्तेमाल करने पर जल्दी खराब न होना
terms.everyday_image: कई हाथों से गुजरने पर भी इस्तेमाल लायक सिक्का

why_chain.step: Money needs to survive repeated exchanges.
Resistance to wear keeps it usable instead of requiring frequent replacement.

unpack.example_or_place: A coin repeatedly used at shop counters.
unpack.consequence: Durability supports continued circulation but does not guarantee stable buying power.
unpack.visual_verb: Pass the same coin through successive hands.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish physical survival from the store-of-value function.

numbers.what: successive payments using the same coin

steps.step: A buyer passes a usable ₹10 coin to a vegetable seller.
steps.mechanism_link: The money withstands handling during a transaction.

steps.step: The seller later passes that usable coin to a tea seller.
steps.mechanism_link: Physical persistence allows repeated circulation.

real_world_example.term_after: The ability to remain usable through handling is durability.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page's characteristic can be seen in coins circulating through many transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: What is portability?
teacher_understanding.answer: The payment medium can be carried conveniently from one place to another.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the book's test for portability?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes portable money as 'Easy to carry.'

teacher_understanding.question: Why does carrying convenience improve money?
teacher_understanding.answer: Buyers need to make payments in different places. A bulky or heavy payment commodity raises the effort and cost of transacting.

items.exam_note: Portability is ease of carrying, not the ability to split money into small units.

terms.plain_meaning: आसानी से साथ ले जा सकना
terms.everyday_image: अनाज की बोरी के बजाय बटुए में पैसे लेकर बाजार जाना

why_chain.step: Buyers must take purchasing means to where goods are sold.
An easy-to-carry medium reduces the burden of making those purchases.

unpack.example_or_place: A buyer moving from a grocery shop to a vegetable stall.
unpack.visual_verb: Move a small wallet between shops.
unpack.level_extra: Separate portability from divisibility: carrying value and splitting value are different.

steps.step: A buyer carries ₹500 in a wallet and spends ₹200 on groceries.
steps.mechanism_link: A compact payment medium is convenient to take to a seller.

steps.step: The buyer carries the remaining ₹300 to a vegetable stall.
steps.mechanism_link: Easy movement allows payment at another location.

real_world_example.term_after: This convenience in carrying money is portability.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page's characteristic appears when people carry money for purchases at several shops.

items.content: Divisibility: Can be broken into smaller units.

teacher_understanding.question: What does divisibility permit?
teacher_understanding.answer: A monetary amount can be represented in smaller units, so payments need not be made only in large amounts.

teacher_understanding.question: Which phrase defines divisibility on the page?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page says money 'Can be broken into smaller units.'

teacher_understanding.question: How does divisibility help with a small purchase?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smaller denominations or units allow the buyer to pay an exact amount or receive change while preserving the total monetary amount.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does 'broken' not mean tearing a note?
teacher_understanding.answer: The division is of monetary value into usable units; physically damaging a note is not the mechanism of making change.

prerequisites: A total divided into smaller amounts
items.exam_note: Divisibility means smaller usable monetary units, not physical destruction.

terms.plain_meaning: रकम को छोटी-छोटी इकाइयों में बाँटकर दे सकना
terms.everyday_image: ₹100 देकर ₹30 की चीज़ लेना और ₹70 वापस पाना

why_chain.step: Goods have different prices, including amounts below a large denomination.
Smaller monetary units allow exact payments and change.

unpack.example_or_place: Receiving change at a grocery counter.
unpack.consequence: Money works for both small and large transactions.
unpack.visual_verb: Split a total into payment and change.
unpack.level_extra: The total value is preserved when a large denomination is exchanged for smaller denominations.

steps.step: The buyer offers ₹100 for soap priced at ₹30.
steps.mechanism_link: The available denomination exceeds the required payment.

steps.step: The shopkeeper returns ₹70 in smaller units and keeps ₹30.
steps.mechanism_link: Smaller units divide the amount without losing monetary value.

real_world_example.term_after: The ability to make these smaller payments is divisibility.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page's characteristic is used whenever a buyer receives change.

items.content: Uniformity: Every unit has the same value.

teacher_understanding.question: How should uniformity be understood without confusing denominations?
teacher_understanding.answer: Equivalent units of the same denomination have the same monetary value. One genuine ₹10 unit substitutes for another genuine ₹10 unit; this does not equate ₹10 with ₹100.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the book actually say?
teacher_understanding.answer: It states 'Uniformity: Every unit has the same value.'

teacher_understanding.question: Why is interchangeability useful?
teacher_understanding.answer: People need not bargain over each equivalent monetary unit as though it were a different-quality commodity; this simplifies pricing and payment.

items.exam_note: Do not interpret uniformity as saying every denomination has equal value.

terms.plain_meaning: एक ही denomination की इकाइयों का मूल्य बराबर होना
terms.everyday_image: एक ₹10 के सिक्के की जगह दूसरा ₹10 का सिक्का देना

why_chain.step: A seller needs equivalent payment units to be interchangeable.
Equal value for equivalent units avoids separate valuation of each one.

unpack.example_or_place: Two genuine ₹10 coins used for identical-priced purchases.
unpack.consequence: Equivalent monetary units can substitute for one another.
unpack.visual_verb: Swap equal-denomination units under an unchanged price tag.
unpack.level_extra: The denomination qualification is outside explanation of the book's abbreviated wording.

numbers.what: buyer's number of ₹10 coins after buying tea

steps.step: Tea costs ₹10, and the buyer has two genuine ₹10 coins.
steps.mechanism_link: The available units have the same denomination.

steps.step: The seller accepts either coin for the same cup; one coin remains.
steps.mechanism_link: Equivalent units perform the same monetary payment.

real_world_example.term_after: This interchangeability of equivalent monetary units is uniformity.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page's characteristic is seen when one same-denomination coin substitutes for another.

items.content: Limited supply: Scarcity helps preserve value.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page regard limited supply as desirable?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies scarcity as something that helps preserve money's value.

teacher_understanding.question: How can excessive money relative to goods weaken purchasing power?
teacher_understanding.answer: If spending rises because more money is available while available goods do not rise correspondingly, prices may rise. Each monetary unit then buys less.

teacher_understanding.question: Does limited supply alone guarantee stable value?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Purchasing power also depends on demand for money and the availability of goods and services. The book says scarcity 'helps', not that it guarantees value.

items.exam_note: Retain the qualifier 'helps'; scarcity is not a complete explanation of money's value.

terms.plain_meaning: रकम की उपलब्धता बिना सीमा बढ़ती न जाए
terms.everyday_image: सामान उतना ही हो लेकिन खरीदने के पैसे बहुत बढ़ जाएँ

terms.plain_meaning: उपलब्ध मात्रा सीमित होना
terms.everyday_image: माँगने वाले ज्यादा हों लेकिन उपलब्ध चीज़ सीमित हो

why_chain.step: People need money to retain usefulness for buying goods.
Restraining excessive supply relative to goods helps protect purchasing power.

unpack.example_or_place: An illustrative market with unchanged goods but increased spending money.
unpack.consequence: Links the quality of good money to its store-of-value function.
unpack.visual_verb: Increase money beside unchanged goods and reduce what one unit buys.
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer a fixed proportional price effect from every increase in money; the example holds other conditions fixed.

real_world_example.place: Simplified local market; illustrative outside example, not observed Indian data

numbers.what: money spent on the same baskets
price per basket under the stated spending assumption

steps.step: Assume 10 unchanged baskets sell for the entire ₹1000 buyers spend.
steps.mechanism_link: Establish a goods supply and an initial purchasing power.

steps.step: Assume buyers now spend ₹2000 on those same 10 baskets, which all sell at one price.
steps.mechanism_link: More spending against unchanged goods raises the illustrative price; ₹200 buys fewer baskets.

real_world_example.term_after: The example explains why limited supply can help preserve money's value.

items.exam_note: The following four items carry each function and its example.

items.content: 1. Medium of exchange: Eliminates the need for barter. Example: You buy groceries using ₹500 instead of exchanging wheat for rice.

teacher_understanding.question: What role does money perform as a medium of exchange?
teacher_understanding.answer: It pays for goods instead of requiring a direct exchange of one good for another.

teacher_understanding.question: Which example identifies this function?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page contrasts buying groceries using ₹500 with exchanging wheat for rice.

teacher_understanding.question: How does money remove a difficulty of barter?
teacher_understanding.answer: In barter, a wheat holder seeking rice must find a rice holder willing to take wheat. With accepted money, selling wheat and buying rice can involve different people.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does separating the two trades help?
teacher_understanding.answer: The buyer no longer has to find one partner whose wants exactly match the goods the buyer can offer. Money connects otherwise separate exchanges.

items.exam_note: Spot a completed purchase; do not confuse payment with merely quoting a price.

terms.plain_meaning: एक सामान के बदले दूसरा सामान देना
terms.everyday_image: गेहूँ देकर चावल लेना

terms.plain_meaning: सामान के लेन-देन में बीच का भुगतान साधन
terms.everyday_image: पहले सामान बेचकर पैसे पाना, फिर पैसे से दूसरा सामान खरीदना

why_chain.step: A person wants goods that another person sells, but their offered goods may not be wanted in return.
Accepted money replaces the need for a direct goods-for-goods exchange.

unpack.example_or_place: The book's ₹500 grocery purchase instead of wheat-for-rice barter.
unpack.consequence: Links back to acceptability and forward to why barter is inconvenient.
unpack.visual_verb: Replace the goods-for-goods arrow with payment and delivery.
unpack.level_extra: The standard name for the barter difficulty is double coincidence of wants; this explanation is outside the page.

real_world_example.place: Grocery shop; book amount with illustrative outside transaction details

numbers.what: grocer's cash received for this purchase

steps.step: The buyer selects groceries priced at ₹500 without offering wheat to the grocer.
steps.mechanism_link: The exchange does not require goods that the grocer personally wants.

steps.step: The grocer accepts ₹500 and gives the groceries.
steps.mechanism_link: Accepted money mediates the exchange.

real_world_example.term_after: Here money performs the medium-of-exchange function.
real_world_example.real_life_link: This is the page's own grocery-purchase example.

items.content: 2. Unit of account: Provides a common measure of value. Example: A phone costs ₹20,000 and a laptop costs ₹60,000.

teacher_understanding.question: What does money do as a unit of account?
teacher_understanding.answer: It supplies one common measure in which the values of different goods can be expressed.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page illustrate a common measure?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both the phone's ₹20,000 price and the laptop's ₹60,000 price are stated in rupees.

teacher_understanding.question: How do these prices make comparison possible?
teacher_understanding.answer: Using the same unit shows that the laptop costs three times the phone and ₹40,000 more. These are calculations from the printed prices.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this differ from medium of exchange?
teacher_understanding.answer: A price tag measures value even before any sale occurs; handing over money to complete the sale is the exchange function.

items.exam_note: A price quotation illustrates unit of account even if nobody pays.

items.content: 3. Store of value: Allows purchasing power to be saved for future use. Example: Keeping money in a bank account for later expenses.
items.type_note: The proposed timeline mistakes 'later' for a sequence; this line defines a function of money.

teacher_understanding.question: What does store of value allow a holder to do?
teacher_understanding.answer: Keep purchasing power available for future use rather than spend it immediately.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the page's example?
teacher_understanding.answer: Keeping money in a bank account for expenses that will occur later.

teacher_understanding.question: How does saving connect income today with spending later?
teacher_understanding.answer: A person retains an unspent balance and draws on it when a future need arises. Receiving income and buying goods need not happen at the same time.

teacher_understanding.question: Does this function guarantee unchanged purchasing power?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. If prices rise, the same nominal balance buys fewer goods. Money can perform a store-of-value role without being a perfect store of real purchasing power.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this different from deferred payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: Store of value concerns carrying one's resources into the future; deferred payment concerns an obligation whose payment falls due later.

items.exam_note: Distinguish stored balances from future debts; avoid assuming inflation-proof value.

items.content: 4. Standard of deferred payment: Makes future payments possible. Example: Home loans and EMI payments are denominated in money.

teacher_understanding.question: What is a standard of deferred payment?
teacher_understanding.answer: Money supplies the standard in which payments due in the future are stated.

teacher_understanding.question: What examples does the page give?
teacher_understanding.answer: Home loans and EMI payments are denominated in money.

teacher_understanding.question: How does denomination in money help a loan contract?
teacher_understanding.answer: Borrower and lender can specify amounts due on future dates in a shared monetary unit rather than leaving repayment as an unspecified quantity of goods.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this not simply storing money?
teacher_understanding.answer: An obligation is being measured for future settlement; the borrower need not already possess the money that will later be paid.

teacher_understanding.question: What do EMI and denominated mean here?
teacher_understanding.answer: EMI means equated monthly instalment, a scheduled monthly loan payment. Denominated means the amount is stated in a particular monetary unit, such as rupees.
